title: Resistance strikes back
blurb: Your first drug works, then the cell adapts. Find a combination that still works.

brief.simple: Your **first** move will work at first, but then the cancer cell finds a detour and most of that effect fades. Use more moves to keep growth and division down.
brief.student: After your first action, the K562 cell **adapts**: 70% of that first action's effect disappears. Add more actions so the combination still reaches the goal.
brief.deep: Scripted adaptation: the first perturbation's effect in K562 is scaled by 0.3; subsequent perturbations are not adapted. This is an illustration, not a learned model of resistance.

note.simple: The cell rerouted its signals around your first move. Only 30% of its effect is left.
note.student: The cell adapted to your first action (70% of its effect faded). This is scripted to show the idea of resistance, not predicted by the data.
note.deep: First-action effects in K562 are scaled by 0.3 to illustrate adaptive resistance; this is not data-derived.

hints: Your first move fades, so put a weaker move first and stronger ones after.
Hit two different points: for example a growth switch (MTOR, RPTOR) and a division gene (CDK6).
Order matters here: the first move is the one that fades.

debrief.simple: Cancer cells can adapt to a drug, so doctors often use **combinations** that block more than one route at once. That makes it much harder for the cancer to escape.
debrief.student: Adaptive resistance through feedback and bypass signaling is well documented, for example after BRAF inhibition in melanoma, where adding a MEK inhibitor improved outcomes. [@lito2013] [@flaherty2012]
debrief.deep: Real resistance is time-dependent and heterogeneous (selection plus adaptation). Modeling it properly would need time-course perturbation data, a 'time-lapse' world model on the roadmap. [@holohan2013]
